steps.ask: BK and AH both meet the tangent HK. What do they make with it, and what shape is BTHK?
steps.title: Draw BT parallel to KH

lines.text: $BK$ and $AH$ are both perpendicular to the tangent $HK$, so $BTHK$ has four right angles. It is a rectangle.

steps.ask: Which triangle has a right angle at T? Which side is its hypotenuse, and what are the other two sides in terms of r?
steps.title: Use Pythagoras in the right-angled triangle ATB

lines.text: $\hl{1}{|\angle ATB| = 90^{\circ}}$, so the hypotenuse is $[AB]$.

steps.ask: Can a radius be negative? r² is 400, so which root is the radius?
steps.title: Take the positive square root

lines.text: A radius cannot be negative.

problems.note: This time the unknown is an angle, not a length. The tangent only comes in at the last step, but it still gives the 90° at the point of contact that you need.

legend.1: the right angle at the point of contact (90°)

steps.ask: Look at triangle ODC. Which of its sides are radii or half a diameter, and what does that make its shape?
steps.title: Show triangle ODC is equilateral

lines.text: $|CD| = \frac{1}{2}|AB|$ and $|OB|$ is a radius, which is half the diameter, so $|CD| = |OB|$.
$|OC|$ and $|OD|$ are also radii, so all three sides of $\triangle ODC$ are equal.
An equilateral triangle has all angles $60^\circ$, so $|\angle ODC| = 60^\circ$.

steps.ask: CD is parallel to AB. Which angle at O is equal to angle ODC because of the parallel lines?
steps.title: Use the parallel lines

lines.text: $CD \parallel AB$, so the alternate angles are equal.

steps.ask: Triangle AOD has two equal sides. What do you know about its base angles, and how does that give you angle OAD?
steps.title: Find the angle at A in triangle AOD

lines.text: $|OA| = |OD|$ (radii), so $\triangle AOD$ is isosceles and its base angles are equal.

steps.ask: Where does the tangent meet the diameter, and which angle does the tangent theorem give there? What is left in triangle ABE?
steps.title: Use the tangent

lines.text: A tangent is perpendicular to the radius (diameter) at the point of contact, so $\hl{1}{|\angle ABE| = 90^\circ}$.
In $\triangle ABE$ the angles add to $180^\circ$, and $|\angle BAE| = |\angle OAD| = 60^\circ$.

problems.note: Now the answer is an area in terms of r, not a number. The radius is still the height, and the 90° at the point of contact is still what makes it the height.

legend.1: the right angle at the point of contact (90°)
legend.2: the unknown radius r, kept as a letter

steps.ask: A radius meets the tangent at 90°. Which line from P can you use as the height of triangle HSP?
steps.title: Use the radius as the height of triangle HSP

lines.text: A radius meets a tangent at $\hl{1}{90^\circ}$, so the radius from $P$ to $[SH]$ is perpendicular to $[SH]$. It is the height of $\triangle HSP$, with base $|SH| = 58$.

steps.ask: What do the three angles of any triangle add up to? Which two angles of triangle ABC are already given?
steps.title: Use the angles in triangle ABC

lines.text: The angles in a triangle add up to $\hl{1}{180^\circ}$. At $A$ the angle is $\hl{3}{30^\circ}$ and at $B$ it is $\hl{3}{45^\circ}$.

problems.note: The two unknown angles are now written in terms of A, so you set up an equation and solve for A. The angle-sum rule is the same as problem 1, and the right angle is the known angle.

steps.ask: One angle is a right angle and the other two are written in terms of A. What must the three angles add to?
steps.title: Use the angles of a triangle

lines.text: The angles of a triangle add to $\hl{1}{180^\circ}$. The right angle is $\hl{3}{90^\circ}$, so the other two angles add to $\hl{3}{90^\circ}$.

problems.note: Now there are several triangles, and each angle you find is used in the next triangle. The 180° rule is the same as before, applied again and again.

legend.1: 180°, the angle sum of a triangle
legend.2: the unknown angle found in this step (B or C)

steps.ask: Which angle is vertically opposite to A at the crossing? What do vertically opposite angles have in common?
steps.title: Find A

lines.text: $A$ and the $\hl{3}{60^\circ}$ angle are vertically opposite angles, so they are equal.

steps.ask: The top triangle has two known angles now. What do its angles add to, and what does that leave for B?
steps.title: Find B

lines.text: $B$, $A$ and $\hl{3}{75^\circ}$ are the angles of the top triangle. The angles of a triangle add to $\hl{1}{180^\circ}$.

steps.ask: Which angle at k matches the 60° angle at j? What is the angle inside the bottom triangle that is on a straight line with it?
steps.title: Find the angle inside the bottom triangle at line k

lines.text: The $\hl{3}{60^\circ}$ angle at $j$ corresponds to the $\hl{3}{60^\circ}$ angle at $k$. The angle inside the bottom triangle is on a straight line with it.

steps.ask: The bottom triangle has a 120° angle, a 40° angle and C. What do its three angles add to, so what is C?
steps.title: Find C

lines.text: The angles of the bottom triangle add to $\hl{1}{180^\circ}$.

legend.2: the unknown angle α or β

steps.ask: α is opposite the angle SPQ. What do opposite angles of a parallelogram have in common?
steps.title: Find α

lines.text: Opposite angles of a parallelogram are equal, so $\hl{2}{\alpha}$ equals $\hl{1}{|\angle SPQ|}$.

steps.ask: β and the angle SPQ share a side. What do adjacent angles of a parallelogram add to?
steps.title: Find β

lines.text: Adjacent angles of a parallelogram add to $\hl{3}{180^\circ}$.

problems.note: The angles are now expressions in x and y, so each rule gives an equation and you solve them one after the other. The two rules are the same as in problem 1.

steps.ask: (2x − 30)° is opposite the 100° angle. What do opposite angles of a parallelogram tell you?
steps.title: Opposite angles are equal: find x

lines.text: $(2\hl{2}{x}-30)^\circ$ is opposite the $\hl{1}{100^\circ}$ angle, so they are equal.

steps.ask: (x + 3y)° and 100° are next to each other on one side. What do adjacent angles add to, and what does that give you for x + 3y?
steps.title: Adjacent angles sum to 180°

lines.text: $(\hl{2}{x}+3\hl{2}{y})^\circ$ and $\hl{1}{100^\circ}$ are adjacent angles, so they add to $\hl{3}{180^\circ}$.

steps.ask: x is known now. Which equation still has y in it, and how do you get y from it?
steps.title: Substitute x = 65 and solve for y

problems.note: There is no angle now. The parallelogram sits on a grid, and you find a missing corner with the same rule: opposite sides are equal and parallel, so [TQ] is a copy of [FB].

steps.ask: Which side is equal and parallel to [FB]? How far, and in which direction, is T from Q?
steps.title: Use the opposite sides of the parallelogram

lines.text: In $FBQT$, the side $[TQ]$ is parallel and equal to $\hl{1}{[FB]}$. $\hl{1}{[FB]}$ goes straight up 5 units, so $\hl{2}{T}$ is 5 units directly below $Q$.

steps.ask: Where does T sit now? Plot it and check the four corners form a parallelogram.
steps.title: Plot T

lines.text: Plot $\hl{2}{T(-2, 2)}$ and join $F$, $B$, $Q$ and $T$ to see the parallelogram.

steps.ask: PQRS is a square. Which other pair of corners moves in the same way as S to P? Then how far do x and y change?
steps.title: Find the translation that takes S to P

lines.text: $PQRS$ is a square, so $S \to P$ is the same move as $R \to Q$.
The $x$-co-ordinate goes up by $\hl{1}{2 - (-4) = 6}$ and the $y$-co-ordinate goes down by $\hl{1}{11 - 3 = 8}$.

steps.title: Find L using the symmetry about the y-axis

lines.text: $\hl{2}{L}$ is the reflection of $\hl{3}{M(9, 1)}$ in the $\hl{1}{y}$-axis, so $\hl{2}{L = (-9, 1)}$.

steps.ask: L and M sit on the same horizontal line. How do you get the length from their x-values?
steps.title: (i) Find the length of LM

lines.text: $\hl{2}{L}$ and $\hl{3}{M}$ have the same $y$-value, so the length is the difference in $x$-values.

steps.ask: Every point on LM has the same y-value. What is that value, and what kind of line is LM?
steps.title: (ii) Write the equation of LM

lines.text: Every point on $LM$ has $\hl{2}{y = 1}$, so the horizontal line is $\hl{2}{y = 1}$.

steps.ask: How can you find the midpoint of [AB] with only a compass and a straight edge?
steps.title: Construct the midpoint D of [AB]

lines.text: Set the compass to more than half of $|AB|$. Put the point on $A$ and draw an arc above and below the line $AB$.
Keep the same compass width. Put the point on $B$ and draw two arcs that cross the first two arcs.
Join the two crossing points with a straight line. It meets $[AB]$ at its midpoint. Label this point $\hl{1}{D}$.

steps.ask: A median joins a vertex to the midpoint of the opposite side. Which vertex and which midpoint do you join?
steps.title: Draw the median from C

lines.text: A median joins a vertex to the midpoint of the opposite side. Join $C$ to $\hl{1}{D}$.

steps.ask: You need a second median. Which side's midpoint is still missing, and how can you find it?
steps.title: Draw a second median

lines.text: Find the midpoint $\hl{1}{E}$ of $[BC]$ by measuring: $|BC| = 10$ cm, so $\hl{1}{E}$ is $5$ cm from $B$. (Or bisect $[BC]$ with arcs as before.)
Join $A$ to $\hl{1}{E}$.

steps.ask: Where do the medians meet, and what is that point called?
steps.title: Mark the centroid

lines.text: The medians cross at the centroid. Label this point $\hl{2}{O}$.

problems.final: \hl{1}{D} \text{ is the midpoint of } [AB] \text{ and } \hl{2}{O} \text{ is the centroid}

problems.note: Same compass method as problem 1, on a new triangle PQR. There are two midpoints to find, M1 on PQ and M2 on QR, and the medians run from R and from P.

legend.1: a midpoint (M1, M2) of a side
legend.2: the centroid G, where the medians meet

steps.ask: What do you need to draw to locate the centroid, and how many medians are enough?
steps.title: Recall what the centroid is

lines.text: The centroid is the point where the three medians meet. A median joins a vertex to the midpoint of the opposite side, so two medians are enough.

steps.ask: Which arcs find the midpoint of PQ without measuring? Where do the arcs cross?
steps.title: Find the midpoint of PQ

lines.text: Set the compass to more than half of $|PQ|$. Draw an arc above and below $PQ$ from $P$, then the same arcs from $Q$.
Join the two points where the arcs cross. This line cuts $PQ$ at its midpoint $\hl{1}{M_1}$. (Or measure $|PQ|$ and mark half of it.)

steps.ask: Do the same with the arcs at Q and R. Which point is the midpoint of QR?
steps.title: Find the midpoint of QR

lines.text: Repeat the arcs from $Q$ and $R$ and join the crossing points. This cuts $QR$ at its midpoint $\hl{1}{M_2}$.

steps.ask: Which two vertices do the medians come from? Where do the two medians cross?
steps.title: Draw two medians and mark the centroid

lines.text: Draw the line from $R$ to $\hl{1}{M_1}$ and the line from $P$ to $\hl{1}{M_2}$.
These medians cross at $\hl{2}{G}$, the centroid. A third median from $Q$ to the midpoint of $PR$ would pass through $\hl{2}{G}$ too.

problems.note: Same centroid method, but the midpoints come from measured lengths, not compass arcs. Measure each side, halve it and mark it. The rest of the steps are unchanged.

legend.1: a midpoint (D, E) of a side
legend.2: the centroid G, where the medians meet

steps.ask: The centroid needs midpoints. Which side do you halve first, and how do you find its midpoint from its length?
steps.title: Find the midpoint of $[BC]$

lines.text: The centroid is where the three medians meet. A median joins a vertex to the midpoint of the opposite side.
Measure $|BC|=11.7$ cm and mark the midpoint at 5.85 cm from $B$. Call this midpoint $\hl{1}{D}$.

steps.ask: Do the same for side AC. How far from A does its midpoint sit?
steps.title: Find the midpoint of $[AC]$

lines.text: Measure $|AC|=11.1$ cm and mark the midpoint at 5.55 cm from $A$. Call it $\hl{1}{E}$.

steps.ask: Which two medians do you draw? Where do they cross, and must the third median go through that point?
steps.title: Draw two medians

lines.text: Join $A$ to $\hl{1}{D}$ and $B$ to $\hl{1}{E}$. Two medians are enough, since all three pass through the same point.
The centroid $\hl{2}{G}$ is where $[AD]$ and $[BE]$ cross. The third median, from $C$ to the midpoint of $[AB]$, also passes through $\hl{2}{G}$.
